title: What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
gist: After Democrats took both the House and Senate in the midterms, divided government with Trump makes major federal energy legislation unlikely, so the action shifts to permitting reform, oversight, state/local utility regulation, and a wave of local votes restricting data centers.

themes.theme: Divided government limits federal energy law

insights.claim: Democrats won both chambers but are nowhere near a two-thirds majority, so any new climate or clean energy legislation needs Trump's signature, sharply narrowing what can pass before the next election.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Expect legislative gridlock rather than another IRA-style swing in energy policy.

insights.claim: The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act and the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which largely slashed the IRA's incentives, were both passed under unified party control; that condition no longer holds.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Big energy-policy swings have required unified government, so policy risk is now lower at the federal level.

insights.claim: A bipartisan permitting reform bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, is set for a Senate vote on November 9; the White House supports it and it could pass with a handful of Democrats, though Democrats might wait to renegotiate next year.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
entities: Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act
insights.so_what: Permitting reform is the main near-term federal energy catalyst for project build-out timing.

insights.claim: Democratic control of Congress will bring subpoena power and investigations of Trump agencies, with leaders already signaling a focus on EPA's Lee Zeldin over staff and investment cuts.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Oversight pressure may constrain deregulatory moves at EPA.

insights.claim: Democrats swept local control in Pennsylvania, where officials signaled support for renewables and emissions cuts, and took the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years; that body regulates utilities and heavily shapes grid build-out.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Utility regulation shifts at state level can change renewable and grid investment faster than federal policy.

insights.claim: Of 41 local ballot questions about data centers tracked by Ballotpedia, nearly all were set to come down against data center development as of the morning of November 4.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Local political resistance is becoming a real constraint on data center siting.
insights.quote: Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development

insights.claim: Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governorship, ousting Greg Abbott, after campaigning for a law to completely pause data center development, which could affect the state's grid and the broader data center industry if passed.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Texas, a key data center market, faces a tail risk of a build moratorium.

insights.claim: The author argues the voter signals, especially on data centers, mean the broadest effect of the election on energy will fall on the data center industry rather than on federal climate law.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: AI infrastructure build-out faces rising political and permitting friction.
